title: Who do you consider to be the most plausible antagonist in an action/thriller film?

commenti.body:
The most plausible is definitely Max Cady in Cape Fear, the Scorsese version.

Just a random inmate going after his former lawyer after he discovered he wasn't defended as best as he could. Deniro with a southern accent already gives me the creeps.

Hans Gruber in Die Hard.

Dude's just a thief, plain and simple. No complex backstory, no abnormal psychology, no bizarre quirks. Just a greedy bastard who wants some money.

I find that more plausible than most action villains.

Old film, but the Paul Scofield character in The Train.
.
Nazis trying to take over culture by stealing nationally renown 
 paintings is both realistic ( "Nazi looting") :and bone chilling...  

The film has a lot of amazing pyrotechnic action and Burt Lancaster showing both action hero and dramatic chops.

One of my favorite antagonists is the hitman in Three Days of the Condor, played by Max Von Sydow. Similar to Anton Chigurh, a ruthless killer, not afraid to take innocent life. But in the end, >!he let's the protagonist go. Not because of any compassion... But because the job is over. It was never personal, just another gig.!<

I think this can be answered in layers based on how un/grounded in reality the action/thriller becomes.
My first take, most realistic answer is Arno in Uncut Gems (2019.) He's just a loan-shark brother in law and Howard is a gambling addict. Some would say it's a stretch to call a thriller, but if you've seen the Safdie Brothers direct you'd understand why I'd call it one.

Another layer of movies I'd say have very realistic antagonists are the ones where the story is man vs man or man vs society and a large part of the plot is one person's loss of reason. Taxi Driver (1976,) Misery (1990,) Nightcrawler (2014,) and Joker (2019,) all fit this mold and are very grounded in realism.

Finally, without writing or spoiling too much, there are movies like The Shining (1980) where the antagonist is realistic but elements of the story and what turns him bad are not. Then there are movies like Fight Club (1999) that start off in my second layer above but stray from the more simplistic plot at the beginning and lose some credibility the further into the movie you get.
Three days of Condor should be regarded among Chinatown and the long goodbye as one of the best thrillers of the 70s.
